clue.text: Change into suit

blocks.note: first meaning: turn into, as a tadpole turns into a frog
second meaning: look good on, as a colour suits someone

explanation.surface: Someone getting changed into a business suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change into suit' reads as one instruction about clothes; it splits into two separate meanings of one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to grow or turn into something and to flatter a wearer, as in 'that hat becomes you'.

clue.text: Fish, netting strange eels? Wrong, as a matter of fact

definitions.text: Wrong, as a matter of fact

indicators.note: a net catches and holds things, so the fish word surrounds the rest
strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a bass is a fish
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fish catching odd-looking eels seems factually wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the wordplay; 'wrong, as a matter of fact' means wrong in its facts rather than its morals.
explanation.definitionFit: A claim without foundation is groundless, so it is factually wrong.

clue.text: Opener for can with more in? It's full of beans

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter
hipper means more in fashion, more 'in'

explanation.surface: A tin opener working on a can that turns out to be full of beans.
explanation.walkthrough: The beans suggest a tin; 'full of beans' is the idiom for lively and energetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Being cheerful and lively is the meaning of the British idiom 'full of beans'.

clue.text: I had the impression it contributes to theme, though tangentially

indicators.note: each word contributes some of its letters, the answer being formed from parts of them

blocks.note: the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A writer felt something added to the theme, albeit indirectly.
explanation.definitionFit: This archaic past tense means 'it seemed to me', the same as saying one had the impression.

clue.text: Retract stupid, stupid thing when PM finishes

indicators.note: to retract is to draw back, so the word is pulled back the other way
the second 'stupid' describes the word after it as senseless, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: dim means slow-witted
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A politician being told to withdraw a foolish remark.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'stupid' is a synonym to be reversed; the second is an anagram signal working on 'thing'. PM here is post meridiem, not Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The p.m. hours of the day run out at twelve o'clock at night, so this is the moment afternoon and evening end.

clue.text: Her bland piece I trashed as not good for readers

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked, so the letters are broken up and reset

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An editor binned a dull article because readers would not enjoy it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not good for readers' sounds like a verdict on quality; it means impossible to read.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing that cannot be deciphered or made out is useless to anyone trying to read it.

clue.text: Magnificent, like Basie or Ellington?

blocks.note: first meaning: grand, stately
second meaning: titled, since the jazzmen were Count Basie and Duke Ellington

explanation.walkthrough: Count Basie and Duke Ellington were jazz bandleaders whose nicknames are aristocratic titles; the question mark flags the jokey sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means impressive and grand, and also belonging to the aristocracy, as counts and dukes do.

clue.text: Source of report that's the reverse of comfortable and fashionable

indicators.note: the reverse of a word is that word written backwards

blocks.note: snug means cosy and comfortable
hot means currently in fashion

explanation.surface: A news story uncomfortable and unfashionable comes from some source.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' suggests journalism; here it is the loud bang of a firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: The sharp explosive bang of a firearm is called its report, and the firing is what makes it.

clue.text: Number of centuries needed for MCC? 4, perhaps

definitions.text: Number of centuries needed for MCC?

blocks.clueFragment: Number of centuries needed for MCC?
blocks.note: first meaning: MCC as a Roman numeral is 1200, which takes this many hundreds
second meaning: the answer to 4 across, the hour when the clock strikes this number

explanation.walkthrough: MCC suggests the Marylebone Cricket Club and centuries of runs; read as Roman numerals it is 1200, i.e. this many hundreds. The cross-reference is to the time 4 across, which a clock shows as this number.
explanation.definitionFit: The number of hundreds in 1200, and the clock hour at midnight, are both this number.

clue.text: One place for parties that's peerless

definitions.text: One place for parties that's peerless

blocks.clueFragment: One place for parties that's peerless
blocks.note: surface reading: an unrivalled venue for celebrations
setter's reading: political parties meet in a chamber without peers, i.e. not the Lords

explanation.surface: Recommending an unbeatable venue for celebrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peerless' means without equal, but literally it means without peers of the realm; Parliament's other chamber is the House of Lords, where peers sit.
explanation.definitionFit: The elected lower chamber of the UK Parliament seats political parties and has no hereditary or life peers.

clue.text: Revered status of John, George, and Paul, but not Ringo

blocks.clueFragment: John, George, and Paul, but not Ringo
blocks.note: surface reading: three Beatles share some status that the drummer lacks
setter's reading: these are also the names of famous Christian saints, while there is no Saint Ringo

explanation.surface: Three Beatles being honoured while the drummer is left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beatles are a red herring: St John, St George and St Paul are all canonised, but nobody calls Ringo a saint.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition of being a canonised holy person is a revered status in the Church.

clue.text: Take part in imbibing excessively?

indicators.note: the answer is just a part sitting inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An invitation to join a drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the instruction and the definition: to take part in excessive drinking is to go on this.
explanation.definitionFit: A bout of heavy drinking or overindulgence is exactly what taking part in imbibing excessively means.

clue.text: Observe friend returning some computers

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the pair is read from right to left

blocks.note: to spot is to notice
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone watches a friend bring back some borrowed computers.
explanation.definitionFit: Portable computers of the kind used on one's knees are a type of computer, hence 'some'.

clue.text: He put an uncle and three sisters on stage

definitions.text: He put an uncle and three sisters on stage

blocks.clueFragment: He put an uncle and three sisters on stage
blocks.note: surface reading: someone casting family members in a show
setter's reading: Uncle Vanya and Three Sisters are plays by a Russian dramatist

explanation.surface: A family member organising relatives to appear in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: The relatives are play titles: Uncle Vanya and Three Sisters were both written by the same Russian playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian writer authored the stage plays Uncle Vanya and Three Sisters, so he put both on stage.

clue.text: Foolishly grips piece of holly

indicators.note: acting foolishly means without sense or order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone clumsily grabbing a prickly bit of holly.
explanation.definitionFit: A small stem with leaves cut from a plant, such as holly at Christmas, is a small piece of it.

clue.text: Circles location without double parking, in reverse

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the circles and site go around the next letters

blocks.note: two O shapes, as circles
P is the parking symbol, doubled
a site is a location

explanation.surface: A driver circling a spot, avoiding double parking, while backing up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double parking' looks like a traffic offence; it simply means two Ps placed inside OOSITE after the first O.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done the other way round is contrary, the converse; 'in reverse' and this word both mean contrary in direction.

clue.text: Medication in second sequence of deliveries — excess that's spread around

indicators.note: in places one thing within the letters of the next

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a pill is a dose of medicine
in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled

explanation.surface: A pharmacy's second round of deliveries leaves excess medicine scattered about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' suggests the post; in cricket a delivery is a ball bowled, and six make an over.
explanation.definitionFit: Overflow or excess that spreads beyond its original area, like an effect spreading to others, is what the word names.

clue.text: Change in force's related to criminal investigation

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its form, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A shake-up in the police force concerns its detective work.
explanation.definitionFit: Scientific methods applied to solving crimes, such as evidence analysis, are described by this adjective.

clue.text: Item on page, very small piece

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for page
an article is an item

explanation.surface: An item printed on a newspaper page is only a tiny piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the page letter first, before the item.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny fragment or speck of matter is a minute portion of something.

clue.text: Fitting quality of a point, shortly followed by another

indicators.note: shortly means in brief, so the word is cut down to its abbreviation

blocks.note: taken as written
PT is the short form of point
another point, of land: a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A speaker makes one point briefly and then another, showing a sense of fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' means another point, here a geographical one: a ness is a headland, as in Dungeness on the Kent coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of being suitable or appropriate for the occasion is fittingness.

clue.text: Indian oddly selected house in part of US

indicators.note: only the letters in odd positions are chosen to be kept

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters
HO is the abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: An Indian person choosing an unusual house somewhere in America.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a state in the north-western United States, so a part of the country.

clue.text: Section of stairs on side of ship where flight begins or ends

indicators.note: a section is only a cut-out portion, so the outer letters of the next word are dropped

blocks.note: taken as written, then trimmed to its inner part
port is the left-hand side of a ship

explanation.surface: A passenger climbing a ship's stairs on one side, ready to depart.
explanation.walkthrough: A flight of stairs is planted in the surface, but the flight here is a journey by plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Air journeys take off from and land at this facility, so it is where a flight begins or ends.

clue.text: Abridged volume I accomplished having potential to succeed

blocks.note: V is the short form of volume
taken as written
able means skilled, accomplished

explanation.surface: An author shortened a book and thinks it may now sell.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that is workable and capable of working out has a real chance of success.

clue.text: Put in grave situation, I am not there for ever

blocks.note: to inter is to bury, putting a body in a grave
the contraction I'm

explanation.surface: Someone in serious trouble insists they will not be around for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave situation' suggests a crisis; it is literally a position in a grave.
explanation.definitionFit: Something provisional or temporary is in place only for the meantime, so it will not last for ever.

clue.text: Dangerous state in East — heavens above

blocks.note: Rhode Island, an eastern US state, abbreviated RI
the sky is the heavens

explanation.surface: A perilous situation in the East, with the heavens looking down.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'above' puts the first piece on top, so the state comes before the heavens.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hazardous carries a risk of harm or loss, which is what dangerous means.

clue.text: A final piece in concert Elgar arranged for free

indicators.note: the final piece of a word is its last letter
a musical arrangement reworks material, so these letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
last letter
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A closing piece of Elgar at a concert, arranged and performed without charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' looks like 'no charge' in a concert setting, but here it means not captured.
explanation.definitionFit: An escaped prisoner or animal still on the loose is described as free and uncaught.

clue.text: Consecrate as bishop? Not so

blocks.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
not so much means less

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether to consecrate a person as a bishop, and being refused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so' looks like a reply of denial; it stands for less, as in 'not so big'.
explanation.definitionFit: To make holy or sanctify something by a religious rite is to consecrate it.

clue.text: Unaware patent has line I inserted

indicators.note: inserted means put inside, so the line and I go into the other word

blocks.note: patent as an adjective means plain to see
L is the abbreviation for line
taken as written

explanation.surface: An inventor does not know their patent has had a line added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patent' suggests an invention; it is the adjective meaning evident.
explanation.definitionFit: Being oblivious means having no awareness of what is going on around you.

clue.text: Influence is held by established kind of writer

indicators.note: to be held by something is to be gripped inside it

blocks.note: EST is the abbreviation for established
a say is influence over a decision
taken as written

explanation.surface: An established type of author holds sway in literary circles.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of short prose pieces on a subject is one particular kind of writer.

clue.text: Judge can rule if that is correct, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives up its opening letter

blocks.clueFragment: can rule if that is correct
blocks.note: the first letter of each of these six words

explanation.surface: A judge may rule on a case provided it is correct to do so.
explanation.definitionFit: A reviewer who assesses and pronounces on the merits of a work acts as a judge of it.
